A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, despite the changed title and organization. All 28 pages of v1 and 30 pages of v2, including tables, equations, algorithms and appendices, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 6 and Tables 1–2 report original Majority Vote and Switch Dominance Game simulations, including convergence frequencies, utility and exploitability.

after.justification: Section 6 and Tables 1–2 retain original simulations on both games and report revised Majority Vote results.

M1.justification: Hedge, SAOLH and behavior cloning retain their procedures. BR_BC is renamed Hedge: v1 Algorithm 4 and v2 Algorithm 5 have equivalent sampling and update rules. The added self-play summary does not introduce a method component.

E1.justification: Both evaluate three-player Majority Vote and 30-player Switch Dominance Game against the same fixed opponent strategies. Replacing human-population terminology with meta-strategy terminology introduces no new population or task.

E2.justification: Both compare against SP_scratch, SP_BC and SP_BC_reg, including the same four regularization coefficients. Hedge is the renamed proposed BR_BC method, whose convergence was already reported in v1's text.

E3.justification: The reported Majority Vote payoff scale changes. v1 Section 6 distributes +0.5 across the majority and -0.5 across the minority, giving individual payoffs +0.25/-0.5; v2 uses +0.5/-1. Opponent strategies, learning-rate parameters, utility/exploitability metrics and 300,000-game evaluation size remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 1 refines the existing Majority Vote regularization analysis with distinct convergence outcomes for each coefficient instead of one shared result. This supplies more detailed evidence about convergence sensitivity; the tested coefficients and two-game failure analysis remain the same.

E5.justification: Both report utility means and standard deviations over 10 runs, convergence frequencies over 100 runs, and the best exploiter from 100 runs. No new uncertainty-estimation procedure, seed disclosure or significance test is introduced.

E6.justification: Table 2 changes MV utilities, in units of 10^-2, from -0.50/0.52 to -1.00/1.03 for self-play/proposed methods, and exploitability from -0.50 to -1.00. These accompany the changed payoff scale, not a comparable-setting performance gain. Table 1 changes regularized bad-equilibrium frequencies from 48% for all coefficients to 50%, 46%, 42% and 42%. SDG results and overall findings remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 halves the theoretical majority/minority payoff constructions and adjusts counterexample and lower-bound proof constants accordingly. It also corrects v1 Section 5.2's comparison of average payoff with an unnormalized oracle sum by using the average oracle payoff. The principal bounds and proof arguments otherwise survive regrouping and renumbering.

C1.justification: Both claim equilibrium/self-play insufficiency, conditional equal-share guarantees through opponent-aware learning, and matching lower bounds for symmetric normal-form games. v2 foregrounds equal share and limited opponent adaptivity, but these objectives and restrictions already appear in v1.

C2.justification: v2 Section 4.1 newly argues that a population's average strategy should not adapt quickly to one learner, extending the practical motivation for limited adaptivity. Section 6.2 removes v1's qualification that smaller learning rates can mitigate random convergence failures at a sample-efficiency cost.

D1.justification: v2 omits v1 Section 6.1's explicit uniform initialization for SP_scratch; the appendix still leaves initialization as an input. This is lost implementation disclosure, not evidence of a changed initialization. Learning-rate formulas, hardware and runtime information are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Freund and Schapire (1997) as the source for Hedge. The other cited research and substantive related-work positioning are largely retained; bibliography formatting changes do not constitute additional research coverage.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and substantial portions of the main narrative are rewritten. Preliminaries gain subsections, Section 4 is organized around explicit conditions, guarantees are presented through average payoff, and appendix preliminaries and proofs are extensively regrouped. Terminology changes consistently from human policies to opponent strategies.

P2.justification: Table 1 expands into separate regularization columns, adds the already-described Hedge convergence outcome and displays percentages. Table captions are revised, and a self-play summary algorithm is added to the main text. The overall single-column layout and two-table presentation remain recognizable.

improvement.justification: v2 improves readability through a clearer equal-share narrative and organization, aligns Majority Vote payoff definitions across theory and experiments, and makes regularization outcomes more informative. These gains outweigh the small losses of initialization detail and the learning-rate qualification. The underlying methods, experimental coverage and principal scientific support remain largely unchanged.
